title: Protecting Material Non-Public Information

sections.body: Protecting material non-public information covers the rules and practices that keep confidential, price-sensitive facts about a company or its securities from being used in trading. In the AI sector, such information can include unannounced model capabilities, chip supply agreements, merger talks, regulatory decisions, and litigation outcomes. The site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments, and each one can be affected by MNPI. The scope extends beyond employees to contractors, advisors, and anyone who receives a tip. It also covers the information itself, from its creation to its public disclosure.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for protecting MNPI runs on a mix of access controls, restricted lists, pre-clearance systems, and trade surveillance software. Firms often maintain a wall between deal teams and trading desks, and they log who has access to sensitive documents and models. In AI companies, this extends to model weights, training data, and internal research notes. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect the many policies and platforms that support this work. Human training and clear escalation paths are as important as the technology.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by identifying MNPI, marking it confidential, and limiting its distribution to a need-to-know basis. Compliance teams maintain restricted lists, review employee trades, and run surveillance for suspicious patterns. When a merger or partnership is discussed, the site's 355 M&A filings show how often such events occur, each one triggering a wall-crossing procedure. That procedure brings additional people over the wall only after they acknowledge their trading restrictions. Investigations follow any alerts, and findings are documented for regulators.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance sit at the center of MNPI protection. Regulators such as the SEC and European authorities enforce prohibitions on insider trading and require firms to have policies that prevent misuse. The site's 148 active AI lawsuits illustrate how often disputes arise, and some of those disputes may involve claims about improper information handling. Provenance matters because information can come from a whistleblower, a data leak, or an AI model that was trained on sensitive data. Firms have a fiduciary duty to protect clients and the market, while individuals have privacy rights that must be balanced against surveillance.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon for MNPI protection is shaped by two forces: more AI tools for monitoring and more AI-generated information to monitor. As the site tracks 732 AI tools, the number of channels through which MNPI can travel is growing. Regulators are paying closer attention to how AI models are trained and deployed, which may lead to new disclosure requirements. Firms are likely to adopt automated surveillance that can flag unusual access patterns or trades. The core challenge will remain the same: keeping confidential information out of the wrong hands while allowing legitimate business to proceed.
